title: The peace churches
hookLine: Mennonites, Quakers and Brethren refuse to fight, following Matthew 5:39

lines: A BIBLE AT THE Version BOARD.
cards: A young man stands in front of a version board with a Bible under his arm. He isn't dodging hard work. He'll drive an ambulance, fight forest fires, empty bedpans on a hospital ward.

The one thing he won't do is carry a rifle. When they ask him why, he opens to the Sermon on the Mount and reads a single sentence out loud. Yesterday, Christians who say a war can be just, inside strict limits.
Today, the Christians who answer: not for us. Mennonites, Quakers, the Brethren. The peace churches.

teach.b: The sentence is Matthew 5:39: "But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also."
The peace churches take that as plain instruction for ordinary life, with no exception carved out for war. They point to the night Jesus was arrested.

One of his followers draws a sword, and Jesus answers with yesterday's line, which the peace churches read as a rule for their own lives: "Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword."
Then he walks toward the cross without a fight. Now notice what turning the cheek is not. It isn't running away, and it isn't shrugging.
The person who turns the other cheek is still standing there, face to face.
Paul puts it in one line: "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good."

So the peace churches pair the refusal with action: relief work after floods and wars, rebuilding houses, sitting between two sides of a quarrel. Quakers call their stance a testimony, something a life says out loud.
Christians in the just war tradition read the same sermon and conclude that protecting the weak can sometimes require force. This path won't rank them.
Each side hands the other a hard question: who protects the neighbor, and what does it cost to turn the cheek?
And both hear the same sermon go on: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you."

how: Mennonite, Quaker and Brethren congregations teach nonviolence as part of following Jesus; members have sought to serve as conscientious objectors rather than bear arms, and these churches run relief, rebuilding and peacemaking work.

o: churches that refuse to fight, and work for peace
churches built after a war to honor a peace treaty
churches that never argue among themselves

games.q: you're the young man at the version board. your church reads Matthew 5:39 as a plain command. what do you do?
o: carry the rifle and keep your faith private.
refuse the rifle and offer to serve another way.
games.why: the peace churches teach both halves: refuse to fight, and serve anyway. turning the cheek means staying in the room, not leaving it.

practice: Bring to mind one little conflict you're in right now, a sharp text thread, a roommate, a sibling, and notice the move you'd usually make to win it.

Then picture the peace churches' way: staying there, not striking back and not walking off, and doing one good thing instead, a softer answer, a real question. If you pray, you can hold that person before God.

wordCard.voice: The peace churches. Mennonites, Quakers and Brethren, who read turn the other cheek as a word for all of life, and refuse to fight while working for peace.

orig.note: Greek, Matthew 5:39: to stand against, to resist. "resist not evil."

carryVoice: Your line: the peaceable way. Not running, not striking: still standing there. That's today, done.
